# Introduction {.unnumbered}

::: small

Understanding how ecosystems respond to biodiversity change is a central challenge in ecology (Loreau et al. 2001; Hooper et al. 2012). Species colonize new areas, go extinct, and shift their abundances in response to climate change, land-use change, and interactions with humans (Sala et al. 2000; Tylianakis et al. 2008; Newbold et al. 2015). These changes are often visible and easy to document. However, observable changes in species composition are only the surface expression of biodiversity change (Hillebrand et al. 2018; Blowes et al. 2019). The deeper ecological question is how biodiversity change reorganizes the ecological structure of natural ecosystems.

Ecological structure can be understood as emergent patterns of trait distributions, species interactions, and spatial organization in co-occurring organisms (McGill et al. 2006; Levine et al. 2017; Maynard et al. 2018). These forms of functional organization arise at the community level and cannot be reduced to the sum of individual species characteristics (Tilman et al. 1997; Loreau 2010). The traits species possess, the interactions they form, and the way those interactions are arranged into ecological networks can change even when local species richness remains stable (Hillebrand et al. 2018; Dornelas et al. 2019; Galiana et al. 2019).

A deeper understanding of biodiversity change therefore requires tracing the processes that generate ecological structure, rather than treating structure as a fixed property of biodiversity (Vellend 2010; HilleRisLambers et al. 2012). Biodiversity change is most often documented through metrics such as species richness, compositional turnover, and taxonomic dissimilarity (Magurran 2004; Baselga 2010). While these measures effectively quantify differences among communities, they provide limited insight into the processes that generate and constrain ecological structure (Chase & Myers 2011; Cadotte & Tucker 2017). Ecological structure is not directly coupled to species composition as  it can be conserved under substantial turnover or rapidly reorganized following relatively small compositional changes (Hillebrand et al. 2018; Maynard et al. 2018). To advance the field, it is therefore necessary to move beyond descriptive metrics toward process-based perspectives that focus on how ecological structure is generated and constrained.

The search for a process-based framework to understand structural changes in biodiversity naturally leads to the concept of assembly as an organizing principle (Diamond 1975; Weiher & Keddy 1995; Vellend 2010). Rather than cataloguing species lists, assembly processes describe how species pools and interactions are filtered and combined to produce assemblages with ecological structure (Keddy 1992; Gravel et al. 2011; Kraft et al., 2015). In this work, I recognize a set of layered processes responsible for organizing biodiversity through space and time: evolutionary processes determine which traits exist (Ricklefs 1987; Losos 2011); regional climatic and biogeographic filters determine which traits and species are available locally (Wiens & Donoghue 2004; Svenning et al. 2015); local community assembly determines which species co-occur (Chase & Leibold 2003; HilleRisLambers et al. 2012); and interaction assembly determines who interacts with whom (Vázquez et al. 2009; Bartomeus et al. 2016; Ponisio et al. 2019). This layered view emphasizes which combinations of traits, species, and interactions are possible, and which forms of ecological structure are likely to emerge under given environmental conditions (Lessard et al. 2016; Maynard et al. 2018).

By framing biodiversity change in terms of layered assembly processes, ecology gains a unifying framework that links ecological and evolutionary dynamics (Vellend 2016; Pontarp et al. 2019). Assembly provides a way to connect species turnover to structural change, and to understand how ecological organization is assembled, maintained, and reorganized through space and time. This thesis develops and applies this framework across complementary levels of organization and timescales.

- In Chapter 1, I formalize a trait-based framework for ecological network assembly, focusing on how traits, species pools, and interaction rules jointly shape emergent network structure (Vázquez et al. 2009; Bartomeus et al. 2016; Maynard et al. 2018). Using simulations and null models, this chapter separates the roles of community assembly within trophic levels from the assembly of interactions between trophic levels, providing a methodological foundation for inferring local assembly processes from empirical ecological network observations. Specifically, this chapter asks: (1) whether spatial variation in the relative contributions of community assembly and interaction assembly leads to systematic differences in network structure, and (2) how the relative importance of bottom-up versus top-down assembly processes changes along environmental gradients and shapes network organization.

- In Chapter 2, I expand the trait-based network assembly framework to the regional scale by introducing the concept of functional trophic asymmetry to quantify mismatches between producer and consumer functional trait diversity (Dehling et al. 2014; Schleuning et al. 2016; Marjakangas et al. 2022). By combining trait data, interaction data, and machine-learning-based network reconstruction, this chapter addresses five questions concerning climatic drivers of functional richness, the emergence of functional trophic asymmetry, its geographic distribution across the Neotropics, its modulation by interaction strength, and its relationship with network specialization.

- In Chapter 3, I extend the assembly perspective into deep time, using fossil mammal assemblages and paleoclimatic reconstructions to investigate how long-term climate dynamics drive compositional turnover and structural reorganization (Blois et al. 2013; Finnegan et al. 2015; Lyons et al. 2016). This chapter disentangles the relative roles of directional climate change and climatic instability in shaping biodiversity across geological epochs, evaluating whether different combinations of climatic change magnitude and instability lead to distinct turnover dynamics.

Together, these chapters show how a layered assembly perspective can be used to link species turnover, trait distributions, interaction networks, and environmental change across scales. By moving from description to process, this work demonstrates how ecological structure emerges from interacting assembly mechanisms, and why understanding these mechanisms is essential for predicting the future reorganization of biodiversity under global change (Tylianakis et al. 2008; Vellend et al. 2017).

:::
